text: Jurriaan Andriessen began his art studies at twelve with the decorative painter Anthony Elliger. He won first prize for his graduation work at the Technical School in Amsterdam in 1766 and was accepted that year into the Guild of Saint Luke. He opened a workshop for painted wallpaper, and idyllic, mythological landscapes were his most popular product. Late in the eighteenth century interest in painted wallpaper declined, so he joined Hermanus Numan to paint theatrical scenery, most notably for the Schouwburg of Van Campen. He was a notable teacher too.

Jean Brusselmans developed his own style. Many see him as a representative of Flemish Expressionism, but he refused to join any art movement. He was not well known during his life and had difficulty selling his work. After his death he was recognized as one of the important Belgian painters of the 20th century. His parents ran a sewing workshop in Brussels, and his younger brother Michel became a composer. A 2018 exhibition at the Gemeentemuseum in The Hague showed his work.

Gerard de Lairesse fled Liège in 1664 after an affair with two of his models led to difficulties. He and his wife Marie Salme settled in Utrecht and then moved to Amsterdam, where the art dealer Gerrit van Uylenburgh had discovered his talent. He arrived with his violin. With it he impressed Jan van Pee. He also had skills in poetry and theatre. His treatises on painting and drawing, Grondlegginge ter Teekenkonst of 1701 and Groot Schilderboek of 1707, were highly influential on 18th-century painters.

Constant Permeke moved from Antwerp to Ostend as a child, where his father, a landscape painter, founded the Municipal Museum of Arts. At the Royal Academy in Ghent he met Frits Van den Berghe and the brothers Gustave and Léon De Smet. In 1909 he settled in Sint-Martens-Latem, where he lived as a recluse. He became a leading figure of Flemish Expressionism. The Nazi occupation declared his work degenerate, and he resumed painting in the late 1940s. In 1997 his portrait and one of his works appeared on the Belgian 1,000 franc bill.

Kurt Schwitters is most famous for his collages, which he called Merz Pictures. He was born in Hanover and lived in exile from 1937. His first epileptic seizure, in 1901, kept him out of the army for most of World War I. He studied at the Dresden Academy alongside Otto Dix and George Grosz and began as a Post-Impressionist. Late in the war he worked as a drafter in a factory, and he said that there he discovered his love for the wheel. He also worked in poetry and typography.

Cornelis Springer learned first from his father, the carpenter Willem Springer, and later from several painters. He joined the Amsterdam collective Felix Meritis and won a gold medal for a painting of a church interior in 1847. He is known for watercolors, etchings and drawings of city views and town scenes that he sketched while traveling around the country. In 1865 Belgium awarded him the Order of Leopold. In 1878 he and Jozef Israëls were invited to advise the Ministry of Public Affairs on the plans for the Rijksmuseum.

Alfred Delauney came to Paris at twelve from Gouville in Normandy to work for his uncle Salmon, a print seller. That shop, the Librairie des Beaux-Arts, passed to him in 1850. He etched paintings by Jean-François Millet, and one of those prints, L'Hiver aux corbeaux, is noted as an inspiration to Vincent van Gogh. A collection of his etchings of old Paris appeared in twenty-four plates. He died in 1894.

Alphonse Mucha was the eldest of six children in Ivančice, a small town in Moravia, and all six children had names starting with A. He showed an early talent for drawing and music, and he sang alto and played the violin. His music teacher sent him to the choirmaster Pavel Křížkovský in Brno, but he had no room for him. In Paris he became known for his decorative theatrical posters, particularly those of Sarah Bernhardt. In 1928 he presented the Slav Epic, a series of twenty monumental canvases, to the Czech nation.

Jan Weissenbruch was the older brother of the painters Isaac and Frederik Hendrik Weissenbruch. Like them he studied at the Royal Academy of Art in The Hague. He was one of the founders of the Pulchri Studio and made watercolors, etchings and woodcuts as well as paintings, mostly of cityscapes and church interiors. In 1857 he won his first gold medal at an exhibition in The Hague. In the late 1860s he began to restore paintings, possibly because agoraphobia held him back in the last decade of his life.

Arkhip Kuindzhi's surname comes from his grandfather's nickname, which means goldsmith in Crimean Tatar. His father was a Pontic Greek shoemaker, and the family was poor. Arkhip lost his parents at six and made a living working at a church building site and at a corn merchant's shop. He grew up speaking four languages. Nobody is sure of his birth date. When the St. Petersburg Academy asked, he wrote 1841, then January, and then crossed out the month several times.

Bruno Liljefors painted nature and animals, especially in dramatic situations, and is regarded as the most important Swedish wildlife painter of his time. He also drew some picture stories, which makes him one of the early Swedish comic creators. His brother was the composer and conductor Ruben Liljefors. He studied at the Swedish Royal Academy of Fine Arts. In 1886 he joined the Artists' Union, which opposed the Royal Academy. He later divorced his first wife and married her younger sister Signe.

Barend Cornelis Koekkoek received his earliest tuition from his father, the marine painter Johannes Hermanus Koekkoek. He enrolled at the Drawing Academy of Middelburg in 1817 and moved to Amsterdam in 1822, where he studied for four years at the Academy of Fine Arts. By 1824, at nineteen, he said that he wanted to be a landscape painter. He became known as the Prince of Landscape Painting and counted King Friedrich Wilhelm IV of Prussia, Tsar Alexander II and King Willem II among his clients. He is regarded as the founding father of Dutch romantic landscape painting.

Johann Adam Klein got his first drawing lessons at eight from the landscape etcher Georg Christoph von Bemmel. A few years later he became an apprentice to the copper engraver Gabler, who taught him etching and noticed his talent for animals, so he sent him to the cattle market to sketch. In 1811 he went to Vienna, where during the Napoleonic Wars he drew and etched the soldiers of both sides in great detail. Prince Metternich became his patron and sent him to Hungary to sketch horses. He also traveled to Styria and Italy.

Michael Ancher grew up on Bornholm, the son of a merchant whose money troubles forced him to fend for himself. In 1865 he worked as an apprentice clerk at Kalø Manor, where the painters Theodor Philipsen and Vilhelm Groth, impressed by his early work, encouraged him to take up painting as a profession. He joined the Royal Danish Academy of Art in Copenhagen in 1871 but left in 1875 without graduating. A student friend, Karl Madsen, invited him to Skagen, a small fishing village in the far north of Jutland. There he became a key member of the Skagen Painters.

Robert van Audenaerde studied first with Francis van Mierhop and then with Hans van Cleef in Ghent. At twenty-two he went to Rome and became a disciple of Carlo Maratti. Maratti saw some of his etchings and advised him to devote himself entirely to engraving. He returned to Ghent after about thirty-seven years away. His altarpiece for the high altar of the Carthusians, showing Saint Peter appearing to a group of monks, is considered his best. He died in Ghent in 1748.

Jan Brueghel the Younger was the son of Jan Brueghel the Elder and the grandson of Pieter Bruegel the Elder. He trained in his father's workshop and took it over at an early age, painting much the same subjects in a similar style. Around 1622 he traveled to Milan, where Cardinal Federico Borromeo welcomed him. In what was likely an act of rebellion, he then went to Genoa to stay with his cousins, the Antwerp painters and art dealers Lucas and Cornelis de Wael. He gradually developed a broader, more painterly manner of his own.

Simon de Passe was the eldest son of Crispijn the Elder, who started the van de Passe dynasty of Dutch engravers. He worked in England from about 1616 and is best remembered for his early London print of Pocahontas. In 1624 he moved to Copenhagen as royal engraver and designer of medals, and he stayed there until his death. Later only Crispijn II in the Dutch Republic and Simon in Denmark remained of the family's engravers. Most of the family's engravings were portraits and book title-pages.

Philip James de Loutherbourg was meant for the Lutheran ministry but decided to become a painter and went to Paris in 1755 to study under Charles-André van Loo. His first Salon showing in 1763 drew praise from Denis Diderot. In 1767 he was elected to the French Academy. Later in England he became known for his large naval works and his elaborate set designs for London theatres. He also invented a mechanical theatre called the Eidophusikon. He was a companion of the confidence-trickster Alessandro Cagliostro.

Leon Wyczółkowski began by aiming at historical painting with documentary realism in the detail. After a trip to Paris he changed course and took up the solutions of the French Impressionists, painting dramatic landscapes, nudes and pastoral scenes. For a short while he came under the influence of Symbolism, and around 1900 he darkened his palette. He was a master of flower arrangements and still life, and he portrayed almost the entire art world of Kraków. From 1895 to 1911 he was a professor at the Jan Matejko Academy of Fine Arts.

Joaquín Sorolla lost both parents in 1865, possibly to cholera, when he was two, and his maternal aunt and uncle, a locksmith, raised him. At eighteen he went to Madrid and studied the master paintings in the Prado. At twenty-two he received a grant for four years of study in Rome, where Francisco Pradilla welcomed him. A long stay in Paris in 1885 gave him his first look at modern painting, especially the work of Jules Bastien-Lepage and Adolph von Menzel. He is known for the Spanish sun and sunlit water in his paintings.

Tadeusz Makowski studied classical philology at the Jagiellonian University and at the same time began studying art in Kraków with Jan Stanisławski and Józef Mehoffer. In 1908 he moved to Paris and lived there for the rest of his life. His frescoes attracted a group of Cubist painters led by Henri Le Fauconnier, which had a decisive influence on his work. During the war years he stayed in Brittany, which inspired him to go back to studying nature. Later his favorite subjects were carnivals, fairs and children. He kept a diary from 1912 to 1931.

Louis Glackens began working in the 1890s for Puck, a magazine known for political and social satire, where his humorous depictions of different ethnic groups reflected the melting pot of New York City. His brother was the Ashcan School painter William Glackens. When Puck was sold in 1914, he began to work for Barré Studio and Bray Productions, pioneering some early animation films. He also worked as a book illustrator. Samuel Sorenson Adams hired him to create advertisements for the Joy Buzzer and other novelty items. He was born in Philadelphia.

Alex Mylona took her first painting lessons at eight and later studied at the Athens School of Fine Arts in the workshop of Michael Tombros. She set up a studio in the Denfert-Rochereau area of Paris in the 1960s. The political persecution of her husband Georgios Mylonas under the Greek junta affected her life. She represented Greece at the Venice Biennale in 1960 and showed at the São Paulo Biennial, among other places. She made sculptures in marble, metal and concrete, as well as paintings and prints.

Alexandre Calame went to work in a bank at fifteen because his father had lost the family fortune. After his father fell from a building and died, he had to provide for his mother. He drew small views of Switzerland. In 1829 the banker Diodati, his patron, made it possible for him to study under the landscape painter François Diday. Within months he gave himself fully to art. He became well known, especially in Germany, and the Alps remained his specialty.

August Allebé taught as well as painted, and his early paintings were romantic but his later work leaned toward realism and impressionism. He was a major initiator of Amsterdam Impressionism, which art historians sometimes call the School of Allebé, as a counterweight to the Hague School. In 1870 he became a professor at the Royal Academy in Amsterdam, and in 1880 its director. The RKD lists 179 pupils, and he stayed in correspondence with former students. His cosmopolitan attitude encouraged modern art.

Hans Makart had a passionate and sensual love of colour, but he was a poor draughtsman. His teachers at the Vienna Academy judged him devoid of all talent, and he was forced to leave. In Munich he attracted the attention of Karl von Piloty after two years of independent study, and from 1861 to 1865 he developed his painting style under him. His Lavoisier in Prison, the first picture he painted under Piloty, was timid but drew attention for its colour. He was the son of a chamberlain at the Mirabell Palace in Salzburg.

Isaac Israëls was the son of Jozef Israëls, one of the most respected painters of the Hague School. He showed talent early. At sixteen he sold his painting Bugle Practice to the artist and collector Hendrik Willem Mesdag, even before it was finished. At the Royal Academy of Art in The Hague he met George Hendrik Breitner, who became a lifelong friend. In 1885 he received an honourable mention at the Salon for his Transport of Colonial Soldiers. Starting in 1886 he lived in Amsterdam and, with Breitner, quickly abandoned the academy.

John Varley painted watercolours, practiced astrology and was a close friend of William Blake. In 1819 and 1820 they worked together on Visionary Heads, a book written by Varley and illustrated by Blake. Varley was born in a Hackney tavern, the Old Blue Post, and his parents discouraged his leanings towards art and placed him under a silversmith. At fifteen or sixteen he became a pupil of Joseph Charles Barrow, whose sketching tour to Peterborough turned him into a professional painter. In 1798 he exhibited a sketch of Peterborough Cathedral at the Royal Academy.

Samuel Howitt came from an old Nottinghamshire Quaker family. In early life he lived at Chigwell near Epping Forest, had money of his own and devoted himself to field sports. When he ran into financial difficulties he had to turn to art as a profession, which he had practiced until then as a talented amateur. In London he was for a time a drawing master at Samuel Goodenough's school in Ealing. He exhibited little because he was in such demand as a commercial illustrator, and he mostly confined himself to sporting subjects and illustrations of natural history.

Nicolaes Maes was the second son of a prosperous cloth merchant and soap boiler in Dordrecht. Around 1648 he went to Amsterdam, where he spent about five years in Rembrandt's studio. By December 1653 he was back in Dordrecht and posting the banns for his marriage to Adriana Brouwers, a preacher's widow. In the middle or end of the 1650s he went to Antwerp to study the Flemish artists Rubens, Van Dyck and Jordaens. Later he returned to Amsterdam, where he became the most prominent portrait painter of the final three decades of the 17th century.

Julie de Graag was the fourth of six children and had fragile health as a child. Her mother, a talented amateur painter, passed on a passion for manual work and drawing. At the Royal Academy of Fine Arts in The Hague she studied in a class made up only of women. The art critic Henk Bremmer, with whom she studied perspective, advised her to focus on colour woodcuts. She also did embroidery. In 1904 she moved to Laren and befriended Bart van der Leck.

Georg Pencz joined Albrecht Dürer's workshop in Nuremberg in 1523. Like Dürer he visited Italy, where Venetian art influenced him deeply. In 1525 he was imprisoned with Barthel and Hans Sebald Beham, the so-called godless painters, for spreading the radical views of Thomas Müntzer. They were pardoned soon afterwards and became part of the Little Masters, named for their tiny prints. Back in Nuremberg he painted trompe-l'oeil ceilings in the houses of patrician families. One of them showed workmen raising building materials on a hoist, so the room seemed still under construction.

Jan van Call is said by Descamps to have been born in Nijmegen and to have taught himself to paint. He began by copying landscapes by Jan Brueghel, Paul Bril and Willem van Nieulandt, and he studied the principles of perspective and architecture. He traveled through Switzerland to Italy and spent some years in Rome, where he collected designs of the most picturesque views around the city. He then returned to the Netherlands and settled in The Hague. His drawings are more esteemed than his pictures. He died in The Hague in 1703.

James MacArdell learned mezzotint engraving in Dublin from John Brooks. When Brooks moved to London in 1746, MacArdell and other pupils followed him. There MacArdell gained a reputation as one of the finest mezzotint engravers in the country and engraved portraits of many famous people. He opened a print shop at the Golden Head in Covent Garden, where he published six views of Dublin in 1753. He died in 1765 and was buried at Hampstead.

Jan Chełmiński, also known as Jan van Chelminski, came from Brzustów and entered the Munich Academy of Fine Arts in 1875. He worked throughout Europe, took out British citizenship in 1893, and from 1895 lived in New York. After divorcing his first wife he married Leonie Knoedler, whose brother Roland belonged to the famous New York art dealership Knoedler. In his lifetime he was best known for historical works, especially those about military history and the Napoleonic Wars.

Ludwig von Hofmann was the son of a Prussian statesman who served as minister-president of Hesse and was briefly Trade Minister under Bismarck. He studied at the Dresden Academy and with Ferdinand Keller in Karlsruhe, and in 1889 he attended the Académie Julian in Paris, where Puvis de Chavannes and Paul-Albert Besnard influenced him. From 1894 to 1900 he traveled widely and spent much time at his villa in Fiesole. His love of antiquity and the idea of Arcadia runs through much of his work. He contributed illustrations to the Art Nouveau magazine Pan.

Nicolas Lagneau drew portraits in France between about 1600 and 1650. He liked grotesque faces, which he drew in great detail from models or from his imagination. He usually worked in black and red chalk, sometimes adding blue or yellow gouache. His realism and his stress on expressions, wrinkles and deformities show the influence of Rembrandt's early works. He is not known to have painted. His portrait drawings were widely copied and imitated in his time.

Jean Béraud's father, a sculptor, was probably working on St. Isaac's Cathedral in Saint Petersburg when Jean was born there. The family moved to Paris after his death. He became a student of Léon Bonnat and exhibited at the Paris Salon for the first time in 1872. Recognition came in 1876 with On the Way Back from the Funeral. He painted precise scenes of Parisian life during the Belle Époque, especially its nightlife, in a style between the Salon and the Impressionists.

Before he painted seascapes, Clarkson Frederick Stanfield worked as a sailor. Like his friend David Roberts he first won recognition as a scenic designer at the Theatre Royal, Drury Lane. He was close to the Royal Academy artists Roberts, Edwin Landseer and Daniel Maclise, and to the writer Charles Dickens, with whom he often collaborated. His friends called him Stanny. He was named after the abolitionist Thomas Clarkson, whom his father knew.

Elsie Lower Pomeroy was the daughter of Cyrus B. Lower, a Union Army veteran and Medal of Honor recipient. She grew up in Washington and graduated from the Corcoran School of Art. By 1908 she was working for the USDA, drawing botanical illustrations for its yearbooks. She painted over 280 watercolors of fruits for the department, from common ones such as citrus, apples and strawberries to less common ones such as cherimoyas. Later she was associated with California Regionalism, also called California Scene Painting.

William Merritt Chase is known as an exponent of Impressionism and as a teacher, and the school he founded later became the Parsons School of Design. His father, a businessman, moved the family to Indianapolis and put him to work as a salesman. Chase showed an early interest in art and studied under local self-taught artists. At nineteen he decided to become a sailor, but after a brief three months in the Navy he understood it was not for him. His teachers urged him to go to New York, and in 1869 he enrolled at the National Academy of Design.

Bartolomeo Pinelli lived and died in Trastevere, a poor quarter of Rome, where he was born the son of an artisan who modeled religious statues. He was educated first in Bologna and then at the Accademia di San Luca. His illustrations often showed the costumes of the Italian people, epic poems and popular customs, and Rome is the most frequent setting. In 1807 he produced an album of 36 watercolors, Scene e Costumi di Roma e del Lazio.

Adamo Scultori came from an artistic family in Mantua. His father Giovanni Battista and his sister Diana were artists too. Because the family was close to the artist Giorgio Ghisi, Adamo and Diana were sometimes called by the surname Ghisi. He worked as an engraver and sculptor. Some of his works can be seen at the Cleveland Museum of Art and the Slovak National Gallery. He died in 1585.

John Frederick Lewis lived for several years in a traditional mansion in Cairo and returned to England in 1851. He painted Oriental and Mediterranean scenes in detailed watercolour or oils, often repeating the same composition in each medium. His careful representation of Islamic architecture, furniture and costumes set new standards of realism and influenced the French painter Jean-Léon Gérôme. Unlike many Orientalist painters, he never painted a nude. His wife modelled for several of his harem scenes.

John Martin grew up in a one-room cottage at Haydon Bridge, the fourth son of a former fencing master. His father apprenticed him to a coachbuilder to learn heraldic painting, but a dispute over wages ended it, and he was placed under the Italian artist Boniface Musso instead. In 1806 he moved to London with Musso and married at nineteen. He supported himself by giving drawing lessons and by painting in watercolours and on china and glass. He later became known for vast, dramatic paintings with minute figures set in imposing landscapes.

Gebhard Fugel grew up in Upper Swabia and apprenticed in Ravensburg before he studied at the art school in Stuttgart. While still a student he began to focus on Christian motifs, and in 1885 his painting Christ Healing the Sick received favorable notice at the Kunstverein München. In 1890 he moved to Munich and helped found the German Society for Christian Art. He soon concentrated on altarpieces and large church murals. In 1895 he made a panorama of the Crucifixion for the pilgrimage town of Kevelaer. He is best known as the leading artist of the Crucifixion Panorama in Altötting.

Tintoretto's real name was Jacopo Robusti, and his nickname means little dyer, because his father Battista was a dyer. His contemporaries both admired and criticised the speed with which he painted and the unprecedented boldness of his brushwork. According to his early biographers, his only formal apprenticeship was in Titian's studio, from which Titian angrily dismissed him after only a few days. The two painters remained on rancorous terms afterwards. His work is characterized by muscular figures, dramatic gestures and bold use of perspective. He was born in Venice in 1518.

Jan Stanisławski first studied mathematics at Warsaw University and then at the Imperial Technical Institute in St. Petersburg. He began to learn painting in Warsaw under Wojciech Gerson and enrolled in the School of Fine Arts in Kraków in 1883. In 1885 he continued his studies in Paris under Charles Durand. While based there he traveled to Italy, Spain, Switzerland, Germany and Austria. With Julian Fałat he painted the landscape parts of Wojciech Kossak's panorama Napoleon's Army Crossing the Berezina. In 1906 he became a full professor at the Academy of Fine Arts in Kraków.

Cornelis Bloemaert was trained as a painter by his father Abraham Bloemaert, his brothers and Gerard van Honthorst, but he devoted himself mainly to printmaking, which he learned from Crispijn van de Passe. Around 1630 he was in Paris, where he engraved plates for Michel de Marolles's Temple des Muses, and in 1633 he went to Rome. His workshop there played an important role in spreading Italian art throughout Europe and attracted many young engravers from abroad. Michel Natalis and Gilles Rousselet were among his pupils. He engraved Annibale Carracci's The Holy Family and Rubens's Meleager.

Jacob van Ruisdael is generally considered the leading landscape painter of the Dutch Golden Age. From 1646 he painted Dutch countryside scenes of high quality for such a young man. After a trip to Germany in 1650 his landscapes took on a more heroic character. In his late work in Amsterdam he added panoramas and seascapes in which the sky often fills two-thirds of the canvas. He also produced more than 150 Scandinavian views with waterfalls. His only registered pupil was Meindert Hobbema.

Henri-Gabriel Ibels studied at the Académie Julian with Pierre Bonnard and Édouard Vuillard. When Paul Sérusier gathered his friends and gave them the name Nabis, from a Hebrew word for prophet, Ibels was among them, and he stayed a member from its founding in 1889. The Nabis worked in bright colors and strong contour lines and wanted painting to be a decorative art and part of everyday life. For inspiration he turned to laborers he met in local bistros. He also mastered lithography for book illustrations, sheet-music covers and advertisements.

Johann Ludwig Aberli was the son of a watchman in Winterthur. Heinrich Meyer taught him first, and in 1741 he was accepted at a drawing school, where he worked as a decorative painter. A trip through the Bernese Oberland with Philipp Hieronymus Brinckmann in the mid-1740s stimulated his interest in landscape painting. He later succeeded his teacher Grimm as operator of the school and often took students to Lake Geneva, Lake Biel and Lake Neuchâtel. In the 1750s he set up his own workshop and a publishing company. In 1759 he took his employees to Paris.

Alfred Sisley was the most consistent of the Impressionists in his devotion to painting outdoors, and his work is almost entirely landscape. Series of paintings around Hampton Court on the Thames, the floods at Marly-le-Roi in 1875 and the Gothic church at Moret-sur-Loing are among his most important. He was born in Paris to British parents, the youngest of four children of an affluent merchant. At eighteen he was sent to London to prepare for a career in business. He received little recognition or money in his lifetime and depended on patrons and art dealers.

Eugène Verboeckhoven painted animals and animated landscapes, and he also made portraits and etchings. He studied under his father, the sculptor Barthélemy Verboeckhoven, and in 1816 under Voituron in Ghent. He was a regular participant at the Ghent salons and at the Brussels salons from 1827 to 1860. He traveled to the Ardennes, France, Great Britain and Italy. He was a member of the academies of Brussels, Ghent, Antwerp, St. Petersburg and Amsterdam. He and his pupils appear to have been the last link to a tradition with roots deep in the 17th century.

Franz Xaver Winterhalter grew up as the sixth child of a farmer and resin producer in the Black Forest village of Menzenschwand. After school at a Benedictine monastery he left home at thirteen to train as a draughtsman and lithographer in Freiburg. In 1823 he went to Munich with the support of an industrialist, and a stipend from the Grand Duke of Baden later let him enter the Academy of Fine Arts. Its academic methods made him uncomfortable. He became known for flattering portraits of royalty and upper-class society. His brother Hermann was also a painter.

Cornelis van Noorde grew up above a bakery in Haarlem, where his parents sold bread on the corner of the Kleine Houtstraat. He studied under Frans Decker and later under Tako Hajo Jelgersma. In 1761 he joined the Haarlem guild of painters. In 1772 he helped found the Haarlem drawing academy in the home of Pieter Teyler, and he became its teacher and director. He married Catharina van Seelen in 1783, and the marriage remained childless. He worked as a landscape painter and draftsman.

Franz von Lenbach grew up in Schrobenhausen, where his father was a master mason. After a short apprenticeship with a Munich sculptor he befriended an animal painter, and in 1854 his family reluctantly allowed him to study at the Academy of Fine Arts in Munich. He then became a pupil of Karl von Piloty, and a travel scholarship won in 1858 took him to Rome with his teacher. His portraits of prominent figures from the nobility, the arts and industry gave him a high standing in society. People called him the Painter Prince.

Józef Chełmoński's first drawing teacher was his father, a small leaseholder who administered the village of Boczki. He studied in a Warsaw drawing class and took private lessons from Wojciech Gerson. In 1872 he went to Munich, where he worked with Polish painters around Józef Brandt and Maksymilian Gierymski. Three years later he moved to Paris, where his work gained popularity because its themes seemed exotic to local audiences. He stayed there until 1897, leaving only briefly for Italy and Poland. He painted realistic landscapes and rural scenes.

Toyohara Chikanobu began as a retainer of the Sakakibara clan in Echigo Province. After the Tokugawa Shogunate collapsed, he joined the Shōgitai and fought in the Battle of Ueno, then followed Tokugawa loyalists to Hakodate. His bravery there under Enomoto Takeaki brought him fame. In 1875 he went to Tokyo to make a living as an artist, working for the Kaishin Shimbun and producing nishiki-e prints. He had first studied the Kanō school but turned to ukiyo-e and joined the school of Ichiyūsai Kuniyoshi.

Paulus Potter moved with his family from Enkhuizen to Amsterdam, where he learned painting from his father, Pieter Symonsz Potter. He joined the Guild of Saint Luke in Delft and by 1649 had settled in The Hague next to Jan van Goyen. There he married the daughter of a leading building contractor, who introduced him to the Dutch elite. Amalia of Solms-Braunfels bought his painting The Farmyard. In 1652 Nicolaes Tulp, who owned several of his paintings, invited him back to Amsterdam. He died of tuberculosis in 1654, having produced about 100 paintings.

Johann Ludwig Bleuler trained in the workshop of his father, a landscape painter in Feuerthalen. After travels along the Rhine and a trip to Brussels and Amsterdam, he met his future wife during a stay in Paris. In 1824 he started his own publishing company in Schaffhausen. He soon began a long series of prints showing landscapes and views along the Rhine, a project that occupied him until his death. His major work, Voyage pittoresque aux bords du Rhin et de la Suisse, appeared in 1845 with aquatints colored by hand in gouache.

Édouard Detaille grew up in Picardy in a prosperous military family, and his grandfather had supplied arms to Napoleon. At seventeen he began studying under Jean-Louis-Ernest Meissonier, who instilled in him a taste for accuracy and precision. He debuted at the Salon of 1867 with a painting of Meissonier's studio. A year later he exhibited his first military painting, The Drummers Halt. In 1870 he enlisted in the French Army when the Franco-Prussian War broke out. Accuracy defined his style.

Fernand Léger, the son of a cattle farmer in Normandy, trained as an architect before moving to Paris, where he worked as an architectural draftsman. After military service he enrolled at the School of Decorative Arts, since the École des Beaux-Arts had rejected his application, and still attended the Beaux-Arts as a non-enrolled student. He later described those years as three empty and useless ones. He began to work seriously as a painter only at twenty-five. After a Cézanne retrospective in 1907, his work showed a new emphasis on drawing and geometry.

Franz Marc grew up in Munich, the son of a landscape painter and a devout Calvinist mother. At seventeen he wanted to study theology like his older brother, but after a year of military service he began studying at the Academy of Fine Arts in 1900. Trips to Paris in 1903 and 1907 let him copy paintings in the museums. He became a founding member of Der Blaue Reiter, and his mature works are mostly animals in bright colors. He was drafted at the start of World War I and died two years later at Verdun.

Jean Morin spent his whole life in Paris, where his father Étienne worked as a master painter before dying young. His sister Catherine married the Flemish painter and engraver Matthieu van Plattenberg, and their son Nicolas de Plattemontagne studied under Morin. Van Plattenberg and Morin worked together on publications such as a series of landscapes and marine scenes. Morin is mainly remembered as a printmaker, whose combination of engraving with etching on the same plate became extremely common. His graphic work consists of 118 plates, among them 50 portraits.

Jakob Fürchtegott Dielmann, the son of a Frankfurt gardener, first trained in lithography. He then studied at the Städelschule and in 1835 attended the Kunstakademie Düsseldorf on a scholarship under Johann Wilhelm Schirmer. He focused on genre art but also painted outdoors along the Middle Rhine, the Main and throughout Hesse. In 1841 Gerhardt von Reutern invited him to the artists' colony in Willingshausen, where he created scenes of village life. In the early 1860s he and Anton Burger moved to Kronberg and founded their own colony. He also worked as an illustrator.

Lambertus Antonius Claessens trained first as a landscape painter at the academy in Antwerp, then went to London to study under Francesco Bartolozzi. In 1795 he moved to Amsterdam, where he stayed active until about 1808. There he worked with the engraver Ludwig Gottlieb Portman on a series of portraits of leaders of the French Revolution, and he married the widow of a French miniature painter. He later settled in Paris for the rest of his life. He mainly made reproductive prints after Dutch, Flemish, French and Italian masters.

Jules Breton grew up in Courrières, a small village in Pas-de-Calais, where his father supervised land for a wealthy landowner. His mother died when he was four. After early schooling near Saint-Omer, he met the painter Félix De Vigne in 1842, who persuaded his family to let him study art. He studied in Ghent and Antwerp, and in 1847 he left for Paris to perfect his training at the École des Beaux-Arts. A love of the land and of his native region stayed central to his art throughout his life.

Hans Gude began with private lessons from Johannes Flintoe and by 1838 attended his evening classes at the Royal School of Drawing in Christiania. He became associated with the Düsseldorf school and is best known for landscapes of Norway's mountains and fjords. His work moved gradually from idealized inland landscapes to seascapes and coastal scenes from the 1860s onward. After early collaborations with Adolph Tidemand, because figure painting was difficult for him, he later added figures on his own. He also taught as a professor in Düsseldorf, Karlsruhe and Berlin.

Cornelis Ploos van Amstel studied under Norbert van Bloemen and Jacobus Buys and later joined the Amsterdam artist society Arte et Amicitia. He kept an art cabinet with over 5,000 drawings, including many by Rembrandt, and was mostly known as a collector and copyist of 17th-century artists. With Jacob van der Schley he made a catalog of the art in the Amsterdam City Hall. He also invented a copying technique that could accurately reproduce drawings in pencil, chalk or watercolour wash. His collection was auctioned in 1800 for 109,406 guilders.

Paulus van Liender studied under Cornelis Pronk and was the nephew of Jacob van Liender and the brother of Pieter van Liender. He sat on the board of the Haarlem drawing academy set up in the home of Pieter Teyler van der Hulst. In 1774 he became steller van het model, which let him direct the live model into various positions during drawing sessions. His early drawings were purely topographical and easily confused with his brother's, but he later developed a more romantic style, focusing on ruins and eventually mainly on large forest trees. He died in Haarlem in 1797.

Henri Charles Guérard began studying architecture at the École Nationale Supérieure des Beaux-Arts but gradually turned to painting and engraving. In 1873 he and Paul Gachet took charge of the illustrations for a weekly magazine, and he became a friend of Édouard Manet. He married Eva Gonzalès, a student and model of Manet, and they hosted Paul Cézanne at a farm near Honfleur. She died in 1883 while giving birth to their son. Depressed, he could not work for a long time. Later he created his own Japonisme album.

Théodule Ribot moved to Paris in 1845 after studying at a trade school in Châlons, and found work decorating gilded frames for a mirror manufacturer. He was mostly self-taught as a painter, though he assisted Auguste-Barthélémy Glaize for a time. After a trip to Algeria he returned to Paris in 1851 and kept making his living as an artisan. In the late 1850s he began to paint seriously at night by lamplight, showing everyday subjects in a realistic style. He made his Salon debut in 1861 with four paintings of kitchen subjects, and collectors bought them.
